It did. As it says the First Nation doesn't want any salmon farms on territory they claim. The land claims situation in the Canadian province of British Columbia is complicated as the various nations never signed any treaties like nations in the rest of Canada did.
All it really says is that they have concerns about proximity to other fisheries, but they don't go into detail about what those concerns are. I'm genuinely curious.

Hoo boy, trying to explain 'rez politics'. They are always complicated. The Ahousaht have previously signed an agreement concerning the development of fish farms in their territory with a different company than that planning the present one. What they want is compliance with their opinion of the effect on other natural resources on which they depend and proper control over development in regards to said resources which they believe they are best placed to understand. The effect on the tourist industry from which they benefit is also involved. Screw up badly and no more rich tourists offered the chance to fish.

The previous agreement also guaranteed a certain level of employment to band members. The foreign corporation (Japanese) which proposes to develop the new fish farm offers no such benefits in either employment nor environmental protection. There is also the very political point about land claims and their right to determine what will or will not happen on their land or (disputed) land adjacent to it and having effects on their territory. Putting it in terms that someone unfamiliar with 'rez politics' might appreciate - it's as if there has been a 50 year dispute over who owns land 30 miles to the south of your town (the town or somebody else) and now a corporation from the other side of the world proposes to build a garbage dump there that may or may not leach onto land that the town owns.

If you do a google search on the subject with its various keywords you will find more information. The band website is, by the way, useless. They usually are, but that's another aspect of 'rez politics' that can be hard for many to understand.

The Union Stock Yards was the meatpacking district in Chicago for more than a century, starting in 1865. Primarily due to its proximity to the prairies and the well developed rail infrastructure, Chicago become the "hog butcher for the world" and the center of the American meatpacking industry for decades. The district, around Halsted and 40th, was operated by a group of railroad companies that acquired swampland and turned it to a centralized processing area.

From the Civil War until the 1920s and peaking in 1924, more meat was processed in Chicago than in any other place in the world. Construction began in June 1865 and the Yards closed in 1971, after several decades of decline during the decentralization of the meatpacking industry. The Union Stock Yard Gate was designated a Chicago Landmark in 1972 and a National Historic Landmark in 1981.
